idiom_name: target object + separate read-only data holder (classic structure)
implementation_notes: Language-neutral structure: give the target class a single holder attribute, create it inside the target's constructor, and let the holder's own constructor perform all validation, normalization and defensive copying; the holder exposes one getter per attribute (a setter only where the value genuinely has to keep changing) and no other write path, and the target forwards its reads to it. Keep the holder private to the target and never hand it out - clients read through the target's accessors or, better, through behaviour that computes what they need. In languages that provide a read-only declaration (const, final, val, let, readonly, init accessors, private fields with accessors, records) the holder object is usually unnecessary: use the declaration and write the defensive copies explicitly, and keep the two-object form for cases where several fields must be validated and frozen as one unit, or where the representation must stay hidden from the target's own members.
pitfalls: Giving the holder setters for attributes that never change after construction hands the write privilege straight back.
Returning the holder itself, or a mutable container it owns, from a getter lets callers write the frozen state through the leaked reference.
Keeping a second writable copy of a field 'for convenience' beside the holder: the two drift and the invariant is lost.
Treating the structure as a security boundary - reflection, serialization hooks and unsafe access still write the fields.

Wrong move: Treat every d-pointer as a frozen read-only holder -> Qt-style shared data may intentionally detach and mutate, so a PIMPL can hide representation without enforcing an immutable invariant -> instead state whether the holder is immutable or supports controlled copy-on-write before choosing this pattern.

Wrong move: Move protected or virtual extension points into the private holder -> derived classes can no longer see or override the interface and the hierarchy becomes unusable -> instead keep protected and virtual members on the target and move only private nonvirtual state or behavior.
